ing: frozen ndole leaves, or use collard greens plus a handful of kale
st: If the leaves are bitter and fresh, boil them for 10 minutes in plenty of water and squeeze dry. Frozen or substitute greens only need a quick rinse.
Boil the peanuts in [[3 cups]] water for 20 minutes, drain, then blend with half the onion, [[3 cloves]] garlic and the ginger into a smooth paste.
Simmer the beef with [[2 cups]] water, the salt, bouillon and a little onion for 40 minutes until tender.
Heat [[1/4 cup]] oil in a large pot over medium heat. Fry the peanut paste for 10 minutes, stirring often, so it does not stick.
Add the beef and its broth to the pot with the crayfish. Simmer 10 minutes until the sauce is thick and creamy.
Stir in the greens and cook for 10 minutes.
Heat the remaining [[1/4 cup]] oil in a skillet and cook the remaining onion and [[2 cloves]] garlic for 3 minutes. Add the shrimp and cook until pink, about 3 minutes.
Fold the shrimp mixture into the stew and serve hot with boiled plantains or rice.

ing: or use shredded okazi/gnetum; kale also works
st: Simmer the beef in [[3 cups]] water with the bouillon cube, half the onion and the salt for 40 minutes until tender.
Rinse the eru leaves and spinach well and chop them finely.
Add the chopped eru leaves to the beef and simmer for 15 minutes. Add the spinach.
Break the smoked fish into pieces and add it with the crayfish and the whole chili if using.
Pour in the palm oil and the remaining onion. Do not stir hard; cook 10 minutes uncovered until the oil blends in.
Stir gently, taste and adjust the salt. The dish should be thick with a glossy, orange sheen.
Serve hot with boiled plantains, cassava or garri.

ing: edible food-grade, or 1 tsp baking soda
optional, or a little ground peanut
st: Simmer the beef with [[2 cups]] water, the bouillon cube and salt for 40 minutes until tender.
Boil the taro in water for 35 minutes until very soft. Drain.
Pound or mash the hot taro in a large bowl with a heavy spoon, or use a stand mixer, until it is smooth and stretchy like dough.
Mold the taro into a few mounds on plates and make a shallow well in the top of each.
Dissolve the limestone in [[1/2 cup]] warm water and let it settle. Pour off only the clear liquid.
Whisk the palm oil with the clear limestone water until it turns thick and yellow like mayonnaise, about 2 minutes.
Stir in the crayfish, chili, njansang, and the hot beef broth to loosen to a soup consistency.
Add the beef and spoon the yellow soup into the wells and around the taro. Eat by pinching taro and dipping.
Soak the black-eyed peas in plenty of water for 4 hours or overnight. Rub them to remove the skins and rinse the skins away.
Drain the beans and blend with the onion, chili, salt and about [[1/2 cup]] water into a thick, smooth paste.
Stir in [[1/4 cup]] of the palm oil and the chopped spinach.
Cut banana leaves into squares and run them over a flame or hot water for a few seconds to soften them.
Put a few spoonfuls of paste in the center of a leaf and fold into a tight packet. Tie with kitchen string.
Line a pot with leftover leaves, stand the packets inside, add [[1/2 cup]] water, cover, and steam for 60 minutes. Add water if it dries out.
Unwrap, drizzle with the remaining palm oil and serve hot with ripe plantain.
Season the chicken with [[1 tsp]] salt, pepper, half the garlic and the ginger. Simmer it with the water for 25 minutes until it reaches 165°F (74°C).
Drain the chicken, saving the broth. Heat [[1/2 cup]] oil in a large skillet and fry the chicken pieces until browned, about 8 minutes. Set aside.
Fry the plantain chunks in the same oil in batches for 3 minutes per side until golden. Drain on paper towels.
In a large pot, heat [[1/4 cup]] oil and cook the onion, celery and remaining garlic for 4 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and thyme and cook for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the carrots, green beans and bell pepper with about [[1/2 cup]] of the saved broth. Cook 8 minutes until tender-crisp.
Return the chicken to the pot and stir with [[1 tsp]] salt. Cook 3 minutes, then gently fold in the plantains. Serve warm.

ing: tilapia or catfish, cleaned, cut in steaks
or toasted ground black cardamom, nutmeg, allspice and black pepper
st: Rub the fish with the lemon juice and [[1/2 tsp]] salt and set aside for 10 minutes.
Toast the dry spice mix in a dry pan over low heat for 2 minutes until the aroma rises and it darkens. Careful not to burn.
Blend the toasted spices, onion, garlic, ginger, tomatoes and chili with [[1 cup]] water until it forms a dark paste.
Heat the palm oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the paste and cook for 12 minutes, stirring, until the sauce turns very dark and the oil separates.
Add [[1 cup]] water and [[1 tsp]] salt, bring to a boil, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Lay the fish in the sauce, cover, and cook gently for 15 minutes until the fish flakes easily with a fork.
Serve hot with boiled plantain, cassava or rice.

ing: bone-in, cut in chunks, or lamb
st: Put the goat in a large pot with the garlic, ginger, half the onion, bouillon cube and salt. Add [[3 cups]] water.
Bring to a boil, skim, then cover and simmer for 60 minutes until the meat is getting tender.
Heat the palm oil in a skillet and cook the remaining onion for 4 minutes. Add the tomatoes and thyme and cook for 8 minutes into a thick sauce.
Stir the tomato mixture into the goat pot.
Add the plantain pieces and [[2 cups]] water, plus the whole chili if using.
Cover and simmer gently for 25 minutes until the plantains are soft and the sauce is thick. The goat should be fully tender.
Taste, adjust salt, and serve hot.
In a large bowl, whisk the flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg and salt together.
Add the warm water and stir until you have a thick, sticky batter that drops slowly off a spoon.
Cover with a towel and leave in a warm place for 60 minutes until doubled and full of bubbles.
Stir once to knock out some air.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 350°F (175°C). Test with a drop of batter, which should sizzle and float.
Scoop a golf-ball amount of batter with a wet spoon or squeeze it with your fist, and drop into the oil. Fry in batches without crowding.
Fry for 4 minutes, turning, until deep golden all over.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm.
Soak the skewers in water for 30 minutes so they do not burn.
Mix the ground peanuts, ginger, garlic powder, cayenne, salt and bouillon powder in a bowl to make the spice rub.
Toss the beef strips with the oil, then coat well with half the spice rub. Marinate for 30 minutes.
Thread the beef onto the skewers in a ruffled pattern.
Heat a grill or grill pan to high. Cook the skewers for 3 to 4 minutes per side until browned and cooked through.
Sprinkle the remaining spice rub over the hot skewers.
Serve with the raw onion rings and extra spice for dipping.

ing: frozen, finely chopped; or use spinach and collard
canned, or 1/2 cup red palm oil with 1.5 cups water
st: If using frozen cassava leaves, thaw and rinse them well. Chop finely.
Boil the corn in [[3 cups]] water for 30 minutes until it begins to soften and burst. Do not drain.
Add the cassava leaves (or substitute greens) and simmer 20 minutes.
Add the palm nut cream, sugar, salt and optional smoked fish.
Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the corn is tender and the broth is rich and slightly thick.
Taste and adjust the salt, then serve hot in bowls.
